title: On SFT, RL, and on-policy distillation
headline: Every way to train a language model after pretraining is the same gradient with three dials, and the shape of that gradient in parameter space is what makes a training step fast, safe, or prone to collapse.
abstract: Why the standard pipeline is what it is, where on-policy distillation fits, and how self-distillation goes wrong. Most post-training pipelines are some version of SFT first, then RL. The argument is about which sampling distribution your method gets to compound with, and where the resulting performance ceiling sits. SFT trains on a fixed teacher distribution, so its ceiling is roughly the teacher's; RL samples its own rollouts so improvements compound and the ceiling is set by the verifier. On-policy distillation closes the gap by training on student rollouts graded token by token by a same-family teacher, but it requires tokenizer and recipe match. When no same-family teacher is available, self-distillation conditions the teacher on a hint or the answer, which sharpens the teacher distribution and creates a pivot-token failure mode that needs per-token KL clipping. Working through each method's gradient geometry places them in a taxonomy of sparse versus dense and biased versus unbiased, and shows all four are settings of a single token-level policy gradient with a sampling-policy dial, an advantage-blend dial, and a teacher choice.

images.alt: Three framed pixel-art tug-of-war panels in a row, where the left team pulls in scattered directions and the cart barely moves, the middle team pulls together in a fan and the cart rolls far, and the right team has one huge clay-orange rope yanking the cart off a cliff, showing that SFT, RL, and self-distillation are three different shapes of pulling force and the shape decides the outcome.
images.caption: Three training methods are three shapes of pull: scattered forces that cancel, a coherent fan that moves the cart, and one rope that drags it off a cliff.

images.alt: A pixel-art chart where a sage-green trail rises fast then flattens out under a dashed fence-topped ceiling line while a clay-orange trail starts slow then steepens and crosses above both near the right, with the crossing circled, showing that off-policy methods plateau below the teacher ceiling while reinforcement learning starts slow but is unbounded by it.
images.caption: Off-policy methods plateau under the teacher ceiling; RL starts slow but crosses past it, and that crossing is the tipping point.

images.alt: A row of evenly short pixel-art figures on a stage with one single towering clay-orange bar near the middle, a dashed cap line drawn across near its top and a downward ink arrow over it, showing that one pivot token the teacher loves and the student barely supports dominates the training loss until a per-token clip caps it.
images.caption: One pivot token, far taller than the rest, dominates the loss until a per-token KL clip caps its contribution.

images.alt: Three brass pixel-art control dials on a warm wooden workshop panel with sage-green trim, each clay-orange pointer set to a different angle with inked tick marks, showing that every post-training method is just a setting of three dials for how the data is sampled, who scores each token, and where the teaching comes from.
images.caption: Every method in the post is a setting of three dials: the sampling-policy mix, the advantage blend, and the teacher choice.
